title: Overloading
body:
Two or more functions have the same name

They are told apart by their **parameters**, and the compiler picks which one you meant from
the arguments at the call site.

```c++
int  max(int a, int b);
double max(double a, double b);
int  max(int a, int b, int c);

max(2, 3);        // the first
max(2.0, 3.0);    // the second
max(1, 2, 3);     // the third
```

The number of parameters or their types has to differ. **A different return type is not
enough**: `int f(int)` and `double f(int)` do not overload, they are a
[[Compile Errors|compile error]], because the call `f(2)` gives the compiler nothing to choose
with.

Overloading is resolved entirely at compile time. That is the line between it and
[[Overriding]], which is a subclass replacing an inherited [[Method]] and is decided at run
time. Same-name-different-parameters versus same-name-same-parameters; see [[Overriding]] for
the full table.

Constructors are the case you meet first, since a [[Class]] usually wants a default one and one
that takes initial values. C++ also lets you overload *operators*, which is how a `string`
manages to answer to `+` and `==`.
